items.prompt: Which metacharacter matches any single character (other than a newline by default)?
rubric: `.` is the wildcard for one character.
`*` is a quantifier, not a wildcard, and `^` is an anchor.

items.prompt: Which anchor matches the start of a string (or line in multiline mode)?
rubric: `^` anchors to the start.
`$` anchors to the end, a common mix-up.

items.prompt: What does the quantifier `+` mean after an item in a pattern?

options.label: Zero or one of the item
Zero or more of the item
One or more of the item

rubric: `+` requires at least one occurrence.
`*` allows zero and `?` means optional.

items.prompt: In most regex flavours, what does the shorthand `\d` match?
rubric: `\d` is the digit class, equal to `[0-9]`.
`\s` is whitespace and `\b` is a boundary.

items.prompt: Which syntax creates a capturing group?
rubric: Parentheses create capturing groups.
Square brackets make a character class and braces are quantifiers.

items.prompt: Which of these are quantifiers in regular expressions? Select all that apply.
rubric: `*`, `?` and `{n,m}` control repetition.
`^` is an anchor and `\w` is a character class.

items.prompt: A developer searches a log file for the exact text `3.14` and wants the dot to match only a literal period, not any character. Which pattern does this?
rubric: A backslash escapes the dot so it is literal.
An unescaped `.` matches any character, e.g. `3x14`.

items.prompt: Which string does the pattern `^cat$` match in full?
rubric: Both anchors force the whole string to be exactly `cat`.
Other options contain `cat` but not as the entire string.

items.prompt: Which pair of strings are both matched by `colou?r`?
rubric: `u?` makes the `u` optional, so zero or one `u` is allowed.
`colr` lacks the `o` and `colouur` has two `u`s.

items.prompt: How does the pattern `[abc]` differ from the pattern `abc`?

options.label: `[abc]` matches a, b, c in that sequence, while `abc` matches any one single letter from those three
`[abc]` and `abc` match exactly the same text because the order of the letters does not matter
`[abc]` matches only the first letter a, while `abc` matches all three letters in any order at all
`[abc]` matches one character that is a, b or c, while `abc` needs a, b, c in sequence

rubric: A character class matches one character from a set.
Plain `abc` is a literal sequence; the distractors confuse order and sets.

items.prompt: The pattern `<.+>` is applied to the text `bold`. What does it match by default (greedy)?
rubric: Greedy `.+` expands as far as possible, ending at the last `>`.
`<b>` would be the result of a lazy `.+?`.

items.prompt: How many matches does `\bcat\b` find in the text `cat concat cats`?
rubric: Only the standalone `cat` has word boundaries on both sides.
`concat` and `cats` have no boundary on one side.

items.prompt: Which strings are matched in full by `^\d{3}-\d{4}$`? Select all that apply.
rubric: The pattern needs exactly three digits, a hyphen, then exactly four digits.
`5551234` lacks the hyphen and `555-12345` has too many digits.

items.prompt: A user applies find-and-replace with regex in an editor. The pattern is `(\w+) (\w+)` and the replacement is `$2 $1`, where `$1` and `$2` refer to the first and second groups. The input text is `Ada Lovelace`. What is the result?
rubric: Group 1 captures `Ada`, group 2 captures `Lovelace`, and the replacement swaps them.
Distractors ignore the group references or repeat one group.

items.prompt: What does the pattern `\d{3}` match?

options.label: The letter d followed by the number 3
Exactly three digit characters in a row
The digit 3 repeated any number of times

rubric: `\d` is a digit and `{3}` means exactly three repetitions.
Distractors treat `\d` as a literal d or confuse `{3}` with the digit 3.

items.prompt: What does the anchor `$` do in the pattern `cat$`?

options.label: It matches cat only when it is at the end
It matches cat followed by a dollar sign
It matches cat followed by any ending text
It matches cat only at the start of the text

rubric: `$` anchors the match to the end of the text.
Distractors treat `$` as a literal dollar sign or confuse it with `^`.

items.prompt: Given the text `onetwo`, the pattern `.*` returns the whole text as one match. Why?

options.label: The regex engine always prefers the longest possible match anywhere in the input, regardless of the pattern's quantifiers
`.*` is greedy: it takes as much as possible, then backs off to the last ``
The `<b>` at the start acts as an anchor, so the match must run from the start to the end of the whole string
`.` matches only one character, so `*` repeats the whole `<b>` group until no more tags are left

rubric: Greedy quantifiers expand as far as possible and backtrack only as needed.
Distractors misread `.*` or invent anchoring behavior; `.*?` would give the shorter match.

items.prompt: What does the character class `[^abc]` match?

options.label: Any string that does not contain abc
Any single character except a, b or c
The start of a string followed by a, b or c

rubric: `^` right after `[` negates the class and it matches one character.
Distractors treat `^` as literal or an anchor, or assume it matches whole strings.

items.prompt: How does `(?:ab)+` differ from `(ab)+`?

options.label: Both repeat ab, but the first does not capture the match
The first makes the ab group optional, while the second requires at least one ab
The first matches a and b in either order, while the second needs ab in order
The first matches ab exactly once, while the second repeats it one or more times

rubric: `(?:...)` is a non-capturing group; repetition behaves the same.
Distractors invent differences in repetition, optionality or ordering.

items.prompt: Which strings contain a match for the pattern `colou?r`? Select all that apply.
rubric: `u?` allows zero or one u, so color and colour match.
colouur has two u's and colr lacks the o, so neither matches.

items.prompt: A developer wants to find the file name `a.c` in a list. Their pattern `a.c` also matches `abc` and `a-c`, which surprises them. Which explanation is correct?

options.label: The dot needs a quantifier such as `+` to act as a wildcard
The pattern is case-insensitive by default, so extra names match
The dot matches only letters, so `abc` is expected to match
The dot is a wildcard that matches any single character

rubric: An unescaped `.` matches any single character; `\.` matches a literal dot.
Distractors invent case rules or misunderstand what the dot matches.

items.prompt: Which pattern matches a string that is exactly a five-digit ZIP code and nothing else?
rubric: Both anchors force the entire string to be five digits.
Unanchored or one-anchor patterns still match longer strings such as 123456.

items.prompt: The pattern `(\w+)@(\w+)\.com` is applied to `bob@site.com`. What text does group 2 capture?
rubric: Group 2 is the second parenthesised part, the word after @ and before .com.
Other options mix up group numbering or include text outside the group.

items.prompt: The pattern `(\d{4})-(\d{2})-(\d{2})` is replaced with `$3/$2/$1` in the text `2024-05-17`. What is the result?
rubric: Groups 3, 2, 1 are day, month, year, joined by slashes.
Other options keep the original order or mis-order the groups.

items.prompt: Which pattern matches exactly the words `gray` and `grey`, and nothing else?
rubric: The class `[ae]` allows one of a or e in that position.
`[a-e]` also allows b, c, d; `(ae)` requires both letters; `gra|ey` is an alternation of fragments.

items.prompt: How many matches does `\b\w{4}\b` find in `this is a test of word sizes`?
rubric: The four-letter words are this, test and word; sizes has five letters.
Wrong counts come from ignoring word boundaries or miscounting letters.

items.prompt: Which patterns match the entire string `A12` when tested against the full string? Select all that apply.

You are searching a log for lines that begin with `ERROR`, then one space, then a full date such as `2024-05-17`, as in `ERROR 2024-05-17 disk full`. You want to avoid lines like `NO ERROR 2024-05-17`. Which pattern should you use?
rubric: The `^` anchor, the space and the hyphenated date together fit the required lines.
Dropping the anchor lets mid-line matches through; other options omit the space or the hyphens.

items.prompt: A find-and-replace uses pattern `(\d+)-(\d+)` with replacement `$2:$1` on the text `a 3-14 b 7-8`. What is the result?
rubric: Each match swaps its two captured numbers, and the global replace applies to both pairs.
Distractors keep the original order, replace only the first pair, or mix up the pairs.

items.prompt: Pattern `^(\d{4})-(\d{2})-\d{2}\s+(\w+)` is run on the line `2024-05-17 ERROR disk full`. What does group 3 capture?
rubric: Only the three parenthesised parts are groups, and the third is the word after the whitespace.
Distractors pick other groups or a later word, from miscounting the groups.

items.prompt:
The pattern `<.+?>` is applied globally to the text `

hi

`. How many matches does it find?
rubric:
The lazy quantifier stops at the first `>`, giving `

`, ``, ``, `

`.
Answering 1 assumes greedy matching from the first `<` to the last `>`.

items.prompt: In a language where `find` searches anywhere in the text, which pattern accepts `555-1234` but rejects both `555-12345` and `x555-1234`?
rubric: Both anchors are needed to force the whole string to be the number.
Each distractor has only one anchor, so one of the bad inputs still matches.

items.prompt: Text: `15 USD, 20 EUR, 30 USD`. Which pattern matches exactly `15` and `30`, with the currency code not included in the matched text?
rubric: A positive lookahead checks for ` USD` after the digits without consuming it.
Distractors include the code, look behind the wrong side, or negate the condition.

items.prompt: Which strings does the pattern `^[A-Z]{2}\d{2,3}$` match in full? Select all that apply.
rubric: The pattern needs exactly two uppercase letters followed by two or three digits.
Distractors have too many digits, lowercase letters, or only one letter.

items.prompt: You export a contact list where each line looks like `Lovelace, Ada`. In your editor's regex find-and-replace, groups are referenced as `$1` and `$2`. You want every line to become `Ada Lovelace`. Which find and replace pair does this?
rubric: The pattern must match the comma and space, and the replacement must swap the groups.
Distractors keep the order, omit the space after the comma, or never match because of the comma.

items.prompt: A developer validates emails by searching with `[a-z]+@[a-z]+\.com`. On `jo.smith@mail.com` it reports a match, but the matched text is only `smith@mail.com`. What causes this?

options.label: The `@` is a special character, so it splits the pattern into two separate searches
The escaped `\.` matches any character, so it swallows the dot in the local part
The `+` quantifiers are lazy, so the engine stops at the first position that satisfies the pattern
The class `[a-z]` has no dot, so a match can only begin after the dot in the local part

rubric: The dot is not in the class, so the match starts after it because the search is unanchored.
Distractors blame laziness, `@` or the escaped dot, none of which affects the start.

items.prompt: The pattern `(a+)+$` takes seconds on the input `aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa!` but is instant on `aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa`. What best explains this?

options.label: The `!` is missing from the pattern, so the engine raises an error and retries slowly
The `$` anchor makes the engine rescan the whole string from every earlier starting position
Nested quantifiers let the engine split the a's in exponentially many ways before it fails
The `+` quantifiers are greedy, and greedy matching always scans the string once per character

rubric: Nested `+` quantifiers give exponentially many ways to partition the a's, and all are tried when the match fails.
Distractors blame anchors, greediness or a missing character, none of which explains exponential growth.

items.prompt: A search for the standalone word with `\bcat\b` does not match the `cat` inside `my_cat`, though it matches in `my cat`. What is the cause?

options.label: The `\b` consumes one character, so the underscore is used up before `cat` can match
The `\b` matches only at the start or end of the whole string, so mid-text fails
Boundaries require whitespace on both sides, and an underscore is not whitespace
The underscore is a word character, so there is no boundary between it and `c`

rubric: `\b` marks a change between word and non-word characters, and `_` counts as a word character.
Distractors misdescribe `\b` as whitespace-based, consuming, or limited to string edges.

items.prompt: The pattern `START.*END` finds nothing in the text `START` then a line break, `middle`, a line break, `END`. It works if all three parts are on one line. Why?

options.label: By default `.` does not match a line break, so `.*` cannot cross lines
The `*` quantifier is limited to a single word, so it stops at the first break
The `.*` is greedy and gives `END` back to the remaining text, so it fails
Anchors are implied, so START must be at a line start and END at its end

rubric: Without a dotall or single-line flag, `.` excludes newline characters.
Distractors invent word limits, implied anchors, or a greediness failure.

items.prompt: Pattern A is `(ab)+c(d)` and pattern B is `(?:ab)+c(d)`. Both are run on `ababcd`. How do they differ?

options.label: A fails because a capturing group keeps only the last repetition and the text is rejected
B matches the same text, but its `d` group is empty because non-capturing groups hide later ones
They match the same text, but `d` is group 1 in B and group 2 in A
A matches the whole text, but B matches only `cd` because non-capturing groups cannot repeat

rubric: Both match `ababcd`, but B's non-capturing group takes no number, so `(d)` becomes group 1.
Distractors claim differences in what is matched, which grouping does not change.

items.prompt: A pattern `[A-Z|a-z]+` was meant to match words made of letters. Which statements about it are true? Select all that apply.

options.label: It is equivalent to `[A-Za-z]+` in every case
It matches a mixed-case run such as `aBc`
It matches only words that are all uppercase or all lowercase
It also matches the pipe character `|` as part of a word

rubric: Inside a class, `|` is a literal and the `+` applies to the whole class, so mixed case is fine.
Distractors treat `|` as alternation, which it is not inside brackets.

items.prompt: In Python, a script runs `re.match(r"ERROR (\d+)", line)` on log lines like `2024-05-17 ERROR 500 timeout`. It returns `None` for every line, though each line clearly contains `ERROR 500`. What is the cause and the fix?

options.label: `re.match` only tries at the start of the string, so use `re.search` instead
`\d+` is greedy and swallows the space, so change it to `\d+?` to stop sooner
`ERROR` is case-folded by default, so add the `re.I` flag to match uppercase
The parentheses make the group mandatory, so remove them to make digits optional

rubric: `re.match` anchors at position 0, and the lines start with a date, so `re.search` is needed.
Distractors blame greediness, group syntax or case, none of which causes a failure here.

items.prompt: On a backtracking engine, which pattern can take exponential time to fail on the input `aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa!`?
rubric: Nested quantifiers `(a+)+` can split a run of `a` in exponentially many ways before the engine gives up.
The other patterns have only one way to consume the input, so they fail in linear time.

items.prompt: In Python, `re.match(r'^\d+$', '42\n')` returns a match even though the string ends in a newline. What explains this?

options.label: `re.match` ignores `^` and `$` anchors, so only a prefix of the string is ever checked
`\d` also matches newline characters, so `+` consumes the whole input including the last one
`$` also matches just before a final newline, so the trailing `\n` falls outside the matched text
`+` is greedy and backtracks past `$`, so the end anchor is skipped for the last character

rubric: Without MULTILINE, `$` matches at the end and before a trailing newline, which is why `fullmatch` or `\Z` is safer for validation.
Distractors blame `\d`, `match`, or greedy backtracking, none of which change how `$` is defined.

items.prompt: Both `"[^"]*"` and `".*?"` applied to the text `"a\"b"` (a backslash-escaped quote inside) return `"a\"` instead of the whole literal. What do the two patterns share?

options.label: Both are lazy, so they stop at the shortest quoted piece they can find
Both ignore the backslash, so the first quote after `a` closes the match
Both fail on the backslash because `.` and `[^"]` cannot match that character
Both are greedy, so they run past the escaped quote and then give back too much

rubric: Neither pattern treats `\"` as an escape, so the quote after the backslash ends the match.
Greedy versus lazy is irrelevant here; `[^"]*` is not lazy and still fails the same way.

items.prompt: In a backtracking engine such as Python's `re`, the pattern `cat|category` finds `cat` in the text `category`, while `category|cat` finds `category`. What explains this?

options.label: Alternatives are tried left to right and the first one that succeeds wins, not the longest one
Alternation picks the shortest alternative unless a longer one is listed first in the pattern
The second pattern compiles differently because it begins with a longer literal prefix
Alternation is greedy by default, so it prefers the longest alternative that fits the text

rubric: Perl-style engines take the first alternative that lets the overall match succeed; order controls the result.
Distractors assume a longest-match rule, which belongs to POSIX-style engines.

items.prompt: After matching `(\w)+` against `abc`, group 1 holds `c`. Why?

options.label: A repeated group is overwritten on each iteration, so it keeps only the last capture
The engine reports captures in reverse order, so group 1 shows the last character first
Greedy `+` makes the group capture the final character after backtracking from `abc`
Capturing groups reset whenever the outer match is retried, leaving only the last attempt

rubric: Each iteration of a quantified group replaces the stored capture; to keep all characters, put the quantifier inside: `(\w+)`.
Distractors invent backtracking or ordering effects; no backtracking happens in this match.

items.prompt: The pattern `^[\w.+-]+@[\w-]+(\.[\w-]+)+$` is used to validate email addresses. Which inputs does it accept even though they are not valid addresses? Select all that apply.
rubric: The local-part class allows consecutive and leading dots, and a domain label may end in a hyphen, so those three pass.
`a@x` lacks a dot-separated label and `a@x..org` has an empty label, so the pattern already rejects both.

items.prompt: An engineer counts timeout failures in logs with `ERROR.*timeout`. The count is higher than the alerting system's. One counted line is `ERROR job=7 retry ok; config timeout=30`, which is not a timeout failure. What is the cause of the over-count?

options.label: Without a global flag the pattern matches only the first `timeout`, which skews the total upward
Greedy `.*` returns the longest possible match, so a line is counted once for every `timeout` it contains
`.*` can span unrelated fields, so any later `timeout` on an ERROR line matches
`ERROR` also matches inside longer words such as `ERRORS`, so unrelated lines get counted as errors

rubric: The pattern only requires both words on one line, so `.*` lets a config value satisfy the match; anchor on the message field instead.
Greedy matching does not multiply per-line counts, and the sample line contains neither a plural nor a missing flag problem.

items.prompt: A service lets customers submit their own regexes. The requirement is that worst-case matching time is guaranteed linear in input length, whatever pattern is submitted. Which approach best meets it?

options.label: Rewrite greedy quantifiers as lazy ones, since lazy matching avoids the exponential paths
Run each match in a thread with a 5-second timeout, since that removes the risk of stalls
Cap input length at 1,000 characters, since short strings cannot backtrack badly enough to stall
Use a linear-time engine such as RE2, accepting the loss of backreferences and lookarounds

rubric: Automaton-based engines give a worst-case guarantee; the cost is dropping features that need backtracking.
Length caps, lazy quantifiers and timeouts reduce or contain the damage but do not guarantee linear time.

items.prompt: In Python 3, a `str` pattern must accept only the ASCII digits 0 to 9 in an ID field, with no flags set and no reliance on caller settings. Which class best meets this?
rubric: `\d` on Unicode strings also matches other scripts' decimal digits, whereas `[0-9]` is explicit.
The other options are equivalent to `\d` and share its Unicode behaviour.

items.prompt: You must extract every link target from 2,000 HTML files generated by one template, where each link is written exactly as `<a href="...">`. It is a one-off job whose output will be spot-checked. Which approach best fits?

options.label: Use a targeted regex like `href="([^"]*)"` and compare counts to a grep, since the format is fixed
Load all files into a browser DOM tool, since parsing fidelity matters more than effort in any one-off job
Use a lookbehind-based regex that tracks nested tags, since that makes extraction fully general for HTML
Build a full HTML parser pipeline first, since regex cannot be trusted on markup even from one template

rubric: With a controlled template and a one-off job, a narrow regex plus a count check is the cheapest sound choice.
Regex cannot track nesting, and heavier tooling adds effort the stated criteria do not require.

items.prompt: A signup form enforces a password policy of five rules that product managers change often. Users must be told exactly which rules failed. Which implementation best meets these criteria?

options.label: Use one pattern with an alternation per rule, so the engine reports which alternative matched on failure
Check each rule with its own small pattern, so failures can be named and rules edited one at a time
Write a single negated character class, so every disallowed password is rejected without rule-specific logic
Combine all rules in one lookahead-chained pattern, so a single match call keeps the whole policy together

rubric: Separate checks give per-rule feedback and isolate edits; a regex match returns only pass or fail.
A lookahead chain is compact but cannot say which lookahead failed; alternation and negated classes do not express these rules.

items.prompt: A refactor rewrites `foo(a, b)` to `bar(b, a)` across 300 files. Arguments are identifiers or member chains like `x.y`, there are no nested calls, several `foo` calls may share a line, and 3-argument `foo` calls must stay untouched. Which search pattern best meets this?
rubric: `[\w.]+` covers member chains and cannot cross commas or parentheses, so 3-argument calls and neighbouring calls are not matched.
`.*` spans several calls, lazy `.+?` still swallows `b, c` in a 3-argument call, and `\w+` misses `x.y`.

items.prompt: A team will maintain a date-parsing pattern for years, and several people will add groups over time. Which are sound reasons to prefer named groups such as `(?P<year>\d{4})` over numbered ones? Select all that apply.

options.label: Named groups make lookbehind assertions fixed-width, so the pattern works in more engines
A named group matches faster, because the engine skips bookkeeping that numbered captures require
Replacement strings can use `\g<year>` rather than a position, so pattern edits don't break them
Code that reads `m.group('year')` documents what each captured piece means without consulting the pattern
Inserting a new group earlier in the pattern does not renumber the references that code already uses

rubric: Names decouple code from group order and make both extraction and replacement self-documenting, which suits long-lived patterns.
Named groups give no speed benefit and have no effect on lookbehind width rules.

items.prompt: A payments team must stop card numbers leaking into logs. Missing a real number is far costlier than redacting a harmless long number. Logs show cards as 16 digits, sometimes grouped by spaces or hyphens, and other brands use 13 to 19 digits. Which redaction rule best fits these criteria?

options.label: Redact only the pattern `\d{4}-\d{4}-\d{4}-\d{4}`, since it matches the format the logs usually show
Redact any run of 13 to 19 digits allowing single spaces or hyphens between digits, with no further checks
Redact any 16-digit run with optional separators, since 16 digits covers nearly every card brand in use
Redact only runs of digits that pass a Luhn check, so ordinary long numbers are never altered

rubric: A broad pattern favours recall, which the stated costs demand; extra redactions of harmless numbers are acceptable.
Luhn filtering lets mistyped real numbers leak, and the narrow patterns miss unseparated numbers or non-16-digit brands.

items.prompt: A service runs user-supplied text through a backtracking regex engine with no timeout. Judging worst-case risk on long near-miss input such as 40 `a` characters followed by `!`, which pattern is most dangerous?
rubric: Nested quantifiers over the same characters let the engine split the run of a's exponentially many ways before failing.
The other patterns have only one way to consume each character, so they fail in linear or quadratic time at worst.

items.prompt: A signup form should catch obvious typos without rejecting real addresses, and ownership is verified by a confirmation email anyway. Which validation is the best trade-off?

options.label: A whitelist of the most common mail domains, because it catches typos in the domain part of nearly every address
A local part limited to letters, digits and dots, because unusual characters are rare in real addresses
A loose check like `^[^@\s]+@[^@\s]+$`, leaving real validation to the later step
A strict RFC-style pattern, because an address that fails it is very unlikely to be deliverable

rubric: A loose shape check avoids false rejects, and the confirmation email is the only true proof of validity.
Strict or whitelist patterns reject legitimate addresses such as plus-tagged or less common domains.

items.prompt: You must extract the text of every `<div>` from untrusted HTML pages where divs can nest to any depth, and the output must be correct for all valid pages. Which approach best meets this?

options.label: Parse the HTML into a DOM and walk its div nodes, since nesting needs a real tree

Use a negated-class pattern `
([^<]*)
`, since it avoids backtracking on nested content

Use the lazy pattern `
(.*?)
` with the dot-matches-newline flag, since lazy stops at the nearest closing tag

Use the greedy pattern `
(.*)
` repeated per match, since greedy always spans the full nested block

rubric: Arbitrary nesting needs tree structure that an ordinary regex cannot track, so a parser is the robust choice.
Lazy and greedy patterns pair the wrong closing tags on nested divs, and the negated class skips any div containing a tag.

items.prompt: You need to extract double-quoted string literals from source code. A string may contain a backslash-escaped quote, and unterminated quotes should fail quickly. Which pattern best meets the criteria?
rubric: The alternation consumes either a normal character or a backslash pair, so escaped quotes are handled and each character has exactly one way to match.
The lazy and negated-class patterns stop at an escaped quote, and the greedy one overruns into later strings.

items.prompt: A form requires a password with a digit, an upper-case letter and at least 12 characters, and must tell the user which rule failed. Which design best meets both criteria?

options.label: One pattern of three lookaheads, since a single anchored match is the clearest way to report any failure
One alternation of the three rule patterns, so the branch that matched shows which rule was broken
Three separate checks, one pattern per rule, so each failing check maps directly to its own message
One pattern of three lookaheads, then inspect the capture groups afterwards to see which rule failed

rubric: Separate checks give a one-to-one mapping between rule and message.
A combined pattern returns only pass or fail, lookaheads capture nothing, and an alternation matches when any rule holds rather than reporting which one failed.

items.prompt: The pattern `^(\w+\s?)*$` hangs a backtracking engine on long text that ends in a symbol. Which mitigations would meaningfully reduce the risk? Select all that apply.

options.label: Run it on a linear-time engine such as RE2
Enforce a match timeout and an input length cap

rubric: Removing the ambiguity, using a non-backtracking engine, or bounding time and input size each limits the blow-up.
Lazy quantifiers and case flags do not change how many ways a failing match can be split, so the exponential search remains.

items.prompt: A Python service validates ZIP codes with `re.match(r'^[0-9]{5}$', s)`. A security review finds that `12345\n` (with a trailing newline) is accepted, and the requirement is that any trailing whitespace must be rejected. Which fix best meets the requirement?

options.label: Add `re.MULTILINE`, because it makes `$` match only at the true end of the whole string
Call `s.strip()` first, because it removes the stray newline before the check runs and keeps input tidy
Replace `[0-9]` with `\d`, because it makes the pattern stricter about which characters are allowed
`re.fullmatch(r'[0-9]{5}', s)`, which requires the whole string to match

rubric: In Python `$` also matches before a final newline, whereas `fullmatch` demands the entire string match.
MULTILINE loosens `$`, strip would accept the bad input, and `\d` is broader, not stricter.

items.prompt: Write a pattern that finds ISO dates `YYYY-MM-DD` in free text, accepting months 01-12 and days 01-31, but not when glued to extra digits (for example inside `120240-01-011`). Which pattern meets every constraint?
rubric: Lookarounds on both ends block neighbouring digits, and the alternations restrict month and day ranges.
The other options miss a boundary, allow values like 19 or 00, or let one glued digit follow.

items.prompt: In a replace-all call, you must insert thousands separators into a standalone string of digits (`1234567` becomes `1,234,567`) using only a zero-width match and `,` as the replacement. Which pattern works?
rubric: A comma belongs only where the remaining digits form complete groups of three up to the end, and `\B` avoids the string start.
The other patterns insert at every position with three digits ahead, only before the last group, or also at the start.

items.prompt: Config lines look like `name = value  # note`. A value is either a double-quoted string (which may contain `#`) or a bare token with no spaces or `#`; an optional comment may follow. Which pattern captures the value correctly?
rubric: A closed quoted string or a bare token without space or `#` handles both value forms and leaves the comment out.
The other patterns cut quoted values at `#`, swallow comments containing quotes, or let bare values absorb `#`.

items.prompt: Validate a single DNS label: 1 to 63 characters from letters, digits and hyphen, with no leading or trailing hyphen. Which pattern meets all constraints?
rubric: A lookahead at the start and a lookbehind at the end check both hyphen rules while allowing 1 to 63 characters.

The first option rejects one- and two-character labels, the second checks the end with a lookahead that is always true there, and the third checks the start with a lookbehind that is always true there.

items.prompt: With the ignore-case flag on, find accidentally repeated words, where the repeat may be separated by spaces or line breaks, and `the theme` must not be flagged. Which pattern meets all constraints?
rubric: Boundaries on both sides plus `\s+` and a backreference match whole repeated words across any whitespace.
Without the trailing `\b`, `the them` is flagged; a literal space misses line breaks; dropping both boundaries also matches inside words.

items.prompt: A log line looks like `a=1&id=42&uid=7`. You need to capture the value of the key exactly `id` (not `uid`, `pid` or `user-id`), where a value ends at `&` or whitespace. Which fragments could belong to a correct pattern? Select all that apply.
rubric: The key must be preceded by the line start or a separator, and the value must be a run excluding `&` and whitespace.
`\bid=` also matches inside `user-id=`, and `(.*)` runs past the value.

items.prompt: A team's validator uses `^[\w.+-]+@example\.com$`. Management now wants subdomains of any depth accepted, such as `ops@eu.west.example.com`. It must still reject `ops@evilexample.com` and `ops@example.com.evil.io`. Which revised pattern does this?
rubric: Requiring each extra label to end in a dot lets any depth through while the domain must still end exactly at `example.com`.
The first option allows `evilexample.com`, the second permits only one level, and the third accepts trailing text after `example.com`.
